pages.c06-p05: Describe the bus, star and ring network topologies, including their advantages and disadvantages

q.q: Which feature best describes a WAN?
o: It uses telecommunications links to cover a large geographical area
It covers one building and uses cables owned by the organisation
It is any network where the devices connect using Wi-Fi only
It links the computers in one office but cannot reach the internet
q.why: A WAN is defined by its large area and its use of telecommunications links such as fibre or satellite.

q.q: A computer that is not connected to any network is called…
o: a file server
a router
a standalone computer
a client
q.why: A standalone computer works on its own; its files and printer can only be used on that one machine.

q.q: Who usually owns the cables and switches in a LAN?
o: A telecommunications company
The internet service provider
The organisation that uses the LAN
The local council
q.why: LAN hardware is normally bought, owned and managed by the organisation itself.

q.q: What is the largest WAN in the world?
o: The World Wide Web
A national intranet
The Internet of Things
The internet
q.why: The internet is a worldwide network of networks. The web is a service that uses it.

q.q: Who usually provides the links used by a WAN?
o: The organisation itself, which lays its own cables between sites
The users, who connect their own home broadband to each site
Telecommunications companies, who rent them to the organisation
The school's network manager, who owns the cables in each town
q.why: WAN links such as fibre, telephone lines and satellites are usually rented from telecoms companies.

q.q: Which area would a LAN typically cover?
o: A whole country
One school or office site
Several towns
The whole world
q.why: A LAN covers a small geographical area such as one building or site.

q.q: A bank links its branches in Derry, Omagh and Newry to its head office in Belfast. What type of network is this?
o: LAN
WAN
Standalone
Intranet only
q.why: The branches are in different towns, so the network covers a large area using telecommunications links.

q.q: What is a file server?
o: A device that forwards data only to the computer it is intended for
A powerful computer that stores users' files and controls who can open them
A device that connects a school network to the internet using IP addresses
A circuit board inside each computer that lets it connect to a network
q.why: The other options describe a switch, a router and a NIC.

q.q: What is a network?
o: One computer with a printer and a scanner plugged into its ports
A collection of web pages linked together and viewed in a browser
A powerful computer that stores files and controls who can open them
Two or more devices linked so they can communicate and share resources
q.why: Devices are linked by cable or wirelessly to share files, printers, software and an internet connection.

q.q: Which answer would earn the mark for distinguishing between a LAN and a WAN?
o: A LAN covers a small area such as one building. A WAN uses telecoms links and is very big
A LAN covers a small area such as one building, whereas a WAN covers a large geographical area
A LAN is a network found inside a single computer, whereas a WAN connects separate computers
A LAN uses cables to connect computers, whereas a WAN is a network that is always wireless
q.why: A distinguish answer must compare both sides in the same point. A WAN is not defined by being wireless.

q.q: Which connection media would a WAN typically use?
o: CAT6 network cables and Wi-Fi inside a single building
Fibre optic cables, telephone lines, satellites and mobile networks
Bluetooth links between pairs of devices in one room
USB cables between a computer and its printer
q.why: WANs rely on telecommunications links; CAT6 and Wi-Fi are typical LAN media.

q.q: Why is backing up a network usually more efficient than backing up standalone PCs?
o: Data is held centrally on the file server, so it can be backed up in one process
Networks copy every file to every computer, so a backup is never needed at all
Each user backs up their own computer, so the job is shared between more people
Network files are stored in RAM, which keeps its contents when the power is off
q.why: Central storage means one scheduled backup covers everyone's files.

q.q: Which of these is a disadvantage of a network?
o: Users can log on at any computer in the building
A virus can spread quickly to all the computers
Expensive printers can be shared by all computers
Security can be managed from one central place
q.why: Being connected lets malware travel between machines; the other three are advantages.

q.q: A network slows down mainly when…
o: the shared printer runs out of paper or toner
users log off at the end of the school day
files are stored on the file server, not the PC
many users transfer large files and bandwidth is limited
q.why: Limited bandwidth is shared by all users, so heavy traffic reduces speed.

q.q: Why can a pupil log on at any computer in the school and still open their work?
o: Their files are saved on the file server, not on one computer
Their files are copied onto every computer each night
Their files are stored in the RAM of the switch
Their files are kept on the router's firewall
q.why: Saving to the file server lets users reach their files from any machine on the network.

q.q: How does sharing hardware on a network save an organisation money?
o: Every computer gets its own printer, so nobody has to wait for documents to print
One colour laser printer can be used by every computer, so one is not bought for each
The computers no longer need NICs, so less hardware has to be bought for the network
The file server replaces the need for switches, routers and cables in the building
q.why: Shared hardware means one expensive device serves all users.

q.q: On a network, programs and updates can be installed once on the server. What is the benefit?
o: They run faster because the server uses its own processor for every user
They can no longer be affected by viruses because the server is protected
They can be used even when the server and network have failed
They become available to every machine without installing them on each one
q.why: Installing once saves time and keeps every machine up to date.

q.q: How do networks allow central security?
o: Each user sets up their own password on the computer they use most
User accounts, passwords and access rights are managed in one place
Every file is copied onto every computer, so none can be lost
The switch encrypts all data so passwords are no longer needed
q.why: Central management controls who can see what across the whole network.

q.q: Why is a network manager or technician a disadvantage of having a network?
o: The organisation must pay staff to keep the network running and secure
The technician can see every user's files, so data is always at risk
The technician must reinstall software on every computer every day
The technician has to back up every standalone computer one by one
q.why: Staff cost is an ongoing expense of running a network.

q.q: What may happen if a network's file server goes down?
o: Each computer becomes a separate LAN
The switch takes over storing users' files
The network automatically becomes a WAN
Users may not be able to reach their work
q.why: Work stored centrally cannot be reached while the server is unavailable.

q.q: Which items must be bought when a network is first set up?
o: Graphics digitisers, 3D printers and microphones for each user
Servers, network interface cards, switches, routers and cabling
A separate colour laser printer for every computer on the site
A standalone backup drive and printer for each of the computers
q.why: These set-up costs are a disadvantage of a network.

q.q: Which advantage of a network means everyone works from the same up-to-date information?
o: Software installed once on the server
Users can log on at any computer
Shared data stored centrally
One printer used by every computer
q.why: Files stored centrally can be used throughout the organisation, so there is one up-to-date version.

q.q: Which statement about the World Wide Web is correct?
o: It is the hardware and cables that link networks together
It is another name for a private network such as an intranet
It is a service of linked web pages that uses the internet
It only works on computers that are connected to the same LAN
q.why: The web is content and a service; the internet is the network underneath it.

q.q: What makes an intranet different from the internet?
o: It uses completely different cables and protocols
It cannot show pages written in HTML
Only authorised users of one organisation can log on
It is always faster because it uses fibre
q.why: An intranet is private and needs a username and password, but uses the same technology as the internet.

q.q: Which is an example of the Internet of Things?
o: A spreadsheet that totals a club's monthly fees
A USB flash drive used to carry coursework
A printed timetable pinned to a classroom wall
A smart doorbell that sends video to a phone
q.why: IoT devices are everyday objects with sensors and internet connectivity.

q.q: What does URL stand for?
o: Universal remote link
Unique router location
Uniform resource locator
User resource list
q.why: A URL is the unique address of a web resource.

q.q: Which best describes the internet?
o: The collection of linked web pages viewed using a browser
A worldwide network of networks that carries data between computers
A private network that only an organisation's staff can use
Everyday objects with sensors that send data to their owners
q.why: The internet is the network (hardware and connections); the other options are the WWW, an intranet and the IoT.

q.q: Email and video calls use the internet. Are they part of the World Wide Web?
o: Yes – everything that uses the internet is part of the web
Yes – because they are viewed in a web browser
No – they use the internet but are not part of the web
No – because they do not use the internet at all
q.why: The web is one service of linked pages; email, gaming and video calls are other services using the internet.

q.q: Web pages are written in HTML. Which protocols are used to request them?
o: HTTP or HTTPS
URL or IoT
LAN or WAN
WPA2 or WPA3
q.why: Pages are requested using HTTP or HTTPS. A URL is the address; WPA2/WPA3 secure Wi-Fi.

q.q: NI schools use C2k so pupils can log on and reach class resources at any time. What kind of service is this?
o: The Internet of Things
An intranet
A standalone system
A Bluetooth network
q.why: It is a private, log-on-only network using internet technology.

q.q: Which is a reason the Internet of Things is growing?
o: Devices no longer need any connection to the internet
Every device now needs a separate cable to the router
IoT devices are always protected by strong passwords
Sensors are cheap and more devices have Wi-Fi built in
q.why: Cheap sensors, built-in Wi-Fi and fast broadband have helped the IoT grow.

q.q: Which is a concern about Internet of Things devices?
o: They cannot send any data over the internet
They can only be used inside a single LAN
They need a separate cable to every sensor
Weak default passwords can let devices be hacked
q.why: Privacy of collected data and weak default passwords are the main concerns.

q.q: If the internet is compared to a road system, what does that tell you about it?
o: It moves data but is not the content itself
It is the content that people read and watch
It is private and needs a username to use
It only connects everyday objects with sensors
q.why: The internet carries data; the web pages are the content carried over it.

q.q: A smart thermostat lets you switch the heating on from your phone. Which term describes it?
o: Internet of Things device
Intranet page
World Wide Web server
Standalone computer
q.why: It is an everyday object with a sensor and connectivity that sends and receives data over the internet.

q.q: Which device connects a school LAN to the internet?
o: Switch
NIC
Terminator
Router
q.why: A router connects separate networks and routes data using IP addresses.

q.q: What does a switch do with data it receives?
o: Sends it to every computer on the network
Encrypts it before sending it to the internet
Stores it as a backup on the file server
Forwards it only to the intended computer
q.why: A switch checks where the data is going and sends it only there.

q.q: Why does each computer on a network need a network interface card (NIC)?
o: To store the files that are shared with the other computers
To choose the best route for data travelling across the internet
To let it connect to the network and provide a port for the cable
To forward data only to the computer it is intended for
q.why: The NIC is the computer's connection to the network. Routing is the router's job; forwarding is the switch's.

q.q: What does a switch use to deliver data to the correct device within a LAN?
o: The IP address of each separate network
The URL of each page that is requested
The MAC address of each device's NIC
The password of each user who logs on
q.why: Every NIC has a unique MAC address built in. Routers use IP addresses.

q.q: What does a router read to decide where to send data across the internet?
o: The MAC address on the NIC
The file name of the data
The URL in the address bar
The IP address on the data
q.why: A router reads the IP address and sends data along the best route.

q.q: What is a MAC address?
o: An address given to each web page
An address used by routers between networks
An address stored in the CPU's MAR
A unique address built into every NIC
q.why: The switch uses MAC addresses to send data to the right device.

q.q: A school replaces its CAT5e cables with CAT6. What is the main benefit?
o: CAT6 is made of glass
CAT6 needs no switch
CAT6 carries data faster
CAT6 is wireless
q.why: Both are copper twisted-pair cables; CAT6 carries data faster. Fibre is made of glass.

q.q: Which type of network cable is used for long or very fast links?
o: CAT5e copper
Fibre optic
CAT6 copper
USB
q.why: Fibre optic cable is used for long or very fast links.

q.q: The box a broadband provider gives you is called a 'router'. What does it usually combine?
o: A router, a file server, a printer and a backup storage drive
A router, a small switch, a wireless access point and often a firewall
A switch, a NIC for every device, a modem and a Bluetooth adapter
A router, a 3D printer, a scanner and a wireless access point
q.why: The home router combines several devices in one box.

q.q: What does a firewall do?
o: Forwards data to the right device
Gives each device a MAC address
Filters incoming and outgoing data
Stores files for all the users
q.why: A firewall controls what data can pass in and out of the network.

q.q: A pupil writes: 'A switch connects the school to the internet.' What is wrong?
o: A router connects networks; a switch forwards data to the correct device within a LAN
A NIC connects the school to the internet; a switch stores the files for every user
Nothing is wrong; a switch and a router do the same job inside every school network
A switch connects networks; a router forwards data to the correct device within a LAN
q.why: Examiners look for: switch → within a LAN; router → between separate networks using IP addresses.

q.q: Where does a router sit?
o: Inside each computer, as a circuit board
At each end of a bus network's backbone
At a gateway, where two networks meet
In the centre of a ring, linking each device
q.why: A router sits at a gateway and decides which path data should take.

q.q: What is the purpose of a terminator in a bus network?
o: To speed up the data so it reaches the end of the backbone more quickly
To connect the bus network to the internet through the school's router
To absorb the signal at the end of the backbone so it does not bounce back
To encrypt the data so other devices on the backbone cannot read it
q.why: Terminators stop signals reflecting back along the backbone and causing errors.

q.q: In a star network, what happens if the cable to one computer breaks?
o: Only that computer loses its connection
The whole network stops working
Data travels the other way round
The central switch restarts itself
q.why: Each device has its own cable to the centre, so the fault is isolated.

q.q: Which topology sends data in one direction round a loop?
o: Bus
Ring
Star
Mesh
q.why: A ring passes data one way from computer to computer until it arrives.

q.q: What is a network topology?
o: The way the devices in a LAN are arranged and connected
The speed at which data travels across a network
The rules that control who can log on to a network
The area covered by a network, such as LAN or WAN
q.why: Bus, star and ring are the three topologies you need.

q.q: In a bus network, what happens if the backbone breaks?
o: Only one computer stops
Data goes the other way
The whole network stops
The terminators take over
q.why: All devices share the one backbone cable, so it is a single point of failure.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of a bus topology?
o: A broken cable to one computer stops the network
Data collisions slow it down when traffic is heavy
It needs the most cable of the three topologies
Data can only travel in one direction along it
q.why: Every device shares one cable, so collisions occur. Bus uses the least cable and data can go either way.

q.q: Why is a bus network less secure than a star network?
o: The terminators store a copy of all the data
Data travels in one direction past every device
The central switch sends data to every device
Every device on the backbone can see the data
q.why: In a bus, data passes along the shared cable past all devices. A switch in a star sends data only where it is needed.

q.q: In a star network, what happens if the central switch fails?
o: The whole network stops
Only one computer is affected
Data travels round a loop instead
The backbone carries the data
q.why: All data passes through the centre, so it is the single point of failure.

q.q: Why does a star network cost more to install than a bus network?
o: Each computer needs a terminator at both ends of its cable
Each computer needs its own cable to the central switch
Each computer must be connected to the two next to it
Each computer needs its own router to the internet
q.why: More cable is needed, so it costs more. Terminators belong to bus networks.

q.q: Which is an advantage of a ring topology?
o: A broken cable only affects the computer it is attached to
New computers can be added without disrupting the network
It needs no cables because the devices pass data by radio
No data collisions, because data flows in one direction
q.why: One-way flow means no collisions and steady performance under heavy load.

q.q: A school adds a computer to a ring network. What is the problem?
o: A terminator must be added to each end of the loop
The central switch must be replaced with a larger one
The new computer can only receive data, not send it
The loop must be broken, which disrupts the network
q.why: Adding a device means breaking the closed loop.

q.q: Which topology needs the least cable and is cheapest to install?
o: Bus
Star
Ring
They all need the same
q.why: Bus uses one backbone, so little cable is needed.

q.q: In a bus network, the short cable linking one computer to the backbone fails. What happens?
o: The whole network stops working
The terminators stop absorbing signals
Data collisions stop on the backbone
Only that computer is affected
q.why: Only a break in the backbone stops the whole bus network.

q.q: How is data sent through an optical fibre cable?
o: As pulses of light through glass strands
As radio waves between masts
As electrical pulses in copper wire
As sound waves along a tube
q.why: Fibre uses light pulses travelling along very thin glass strands.

q.q: What must happen before two Bluetooth devices can exchange data?
o: They must be paired
They must be plugged into a router
They must be on a 5G network
They must be given IP addresses
q.why: Bluetooth links two devices directly once they are paired; no router or network is needed.

q.q: Which is a correct statement about 5G compared with 4G?
o: 5G offers much lower latency and higher speeds
5G has higher latency but covers a larger area
Each high-speed 5G mast covers a larger area
5G sends data as light pulses instead of radio
q.why: 5G is faster with lower latency, but each high-speed mast covers a smaller area.

q.q: What does Wi-Fi use to connect devices to a network?
o: Radio waves and a wireless router or access point
Light pulses through a thin glass cable
A direct paired link between two devices
Copper twisted-pair cables to a switch
q.why: Wi-Fi uses radio waves, so no network cables are needed.

q.q: What is the typical indoor range of Wi-Fi?
o: About 1 metre, the length of a short cable
Tens of metres, reduced by walls and floors
Several kilometres from one wireless router
Unlimited, because it uses the internet
q.why: Wi-Fi typically covers tens of metres; Bluetooth covers about 10 m.

q.q: What is the typical range of Bluetooth?
o: About 100 metres
Several kilometres
About 1 centimetre
About 10 metres
q.why: Bluetooth is short-range and low-power, typically within about 10 m.

q.q: Why does Bluetooth cost nothing to use?
o: It sends its data over the mobile network
No router or network provider is needed
It is paid for by the internet provider
It uses the household's Wi-Fi password
q.why: Bluetooth links two devices directly, so there is no network or data plan.

q.q: Why is optical fibre not affected by electrical interference?
o: It carries light, not electrical signals
It is always buried deep underground
It uses radio waves at a high frequency
It is wrapped in a layer of copper wire
q.why: Light is not affected by electrical interference, so fibre is very reliable.

q.q: Why is optical fibre expensive to install?
o: Every glass strand needs its own router
Light pulses need a repeater every metre
Roads or pavements often have to be dug up
The cable must be replaced every year
q.why: Installation needs trenches and specialists. Repeaters are only needed on very long links.

q.q: Why do 5G networks need many more masts than 4G?
o: Each 5G mast can only connect a single phone at a time, unlike 4G masts
5G signals travel through optical fibre rather than through the air
Each high-speed 5G mast covers a smaller area and signals are blocked more easily
5G masts must be paired with each phone before data can be exchanged
q.why: The fastest 5G frequencies have a shorter range, so more masts are needed. Some older books wrongly say the opposite.

q.q: How should a home or school Wi-Fi network be protected?
o: With a terminator at the end of each signal
By pairing every device before it is used
By turning off the router's MAC addresses
With a password and WPA2 or WPA3 encryption
q.why: Radio signals can be picked up in range, so encryption is essential.

q.q: Which is the best description of 4G?
o: Short-range wireless that links two paired devices directly together
Pulses of light sent along glass strands between two buildings
Wireless connection inside a building through an access point
Mobile data through masts, fast enough for HD streaming and video calls
q.why: 4G gives high-speed mobile data; the others describe Bluetooth, fibre and Wi-Fi.

q.q: Which technology is least affected by electrical interference?
o: Wi-Fi
Optical fibre
Bluetooth
4G
q.why: Fibre carries light, which electrical interference does not affect.

q.q: On which criterion is Bluetooth weakest?
o: Cost
Power use
Range
Ease of pairing
q.why: Bluetooth typically works only within about 10 m. It is cheap and low-power.

q.q: Why must Wi-Fi traffic be encrypted?
o: Wi-Fi is always slow unless the data is encrypted before it is sent
Radio signals travel through the air and can be picked up by anyone in range
Encryption makes the range of the wireless router larger in a building
Routers will not switch on until an encryption key has been typed in
q.why: Encryption stops intercepted wireless data being read.

q.q: Which are the five criteria the specification gives for evaluating communication technologies?
o: Capacity, access speed, portability, durability and cost
Speed, size, colour, weight and battery life
Range, latency, pairing, masts and bandwidth
Speed, range, reliability, security and cost
q.why: Capacity, access speed, portability and durability are the criteria for storage devices.

q.q: What is the security risk with Bluetooth?
o: Data is sent along a cable that is easy to tap into
Data is sent through masts owned by the mobile network
Data is sent to every device on the backbone at once
A device left 'discoverable' can be connected to by others
q.why: Bluetooth is a risk if a device is left discoverable.

q.q: Which technology is the slowest of Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, optical fibre and 5G?
o: Bluetooth
Wi-Fi
Optical fibre
5G
q.why: Bluetooth has low speed; fibre has the greatest bandwidth.

q.q: Which is the fastest wireless option for most users?
o: 4G
Bluetooth
5G
Older 54 Mbps Wi-Fi
q.why: 5G has very high speed and low latency.

q.q: Fibre is very reliable. In what situation does it stop working completely?
o: When it rains heavily
When the cable is cut
When it is near electrical equipment
When many users are connected at once
q.why: Fibre is not affected by interference or weather, but a cut cable stops everything.

q.q: Which statement about cost is correct?
o: Fibre is cheap to set up; wireless costs more to install but lasts many years
Bluetooth needs an ongoing data plan; 4G needs no network at all
Wireless is cheap to set up; fibre costs more to install but lasts many years
Wi-Fi needs a 5G-capable phone; fibre needs a data plan for each user
q.why: Wi-Fi needs one router and no cabling; fibre needs trenches but lasts.

q.q: What makes a strong answer to an 'evaluate' question about a technology?
o: A list of every strength of the technology with no weaknesses given
A strength and a weakness linked to criteria, ending with a judgement
A definition of the technology followed by a typical example of use
A statement that the technology is quick and better than the others
q.why: Evaluate questions reward balance and a final judgement for the situation.

q.q: Which is an advantage of wireless over optical fibre?
o: Users can move around while staying connected
It has higher bandwidth over long distances
It is not affected by walls and other devices
Its signals are much harder to intercept
q.why: Mobility is wireless's main advantage. Fibre wins on bandwidth, reliability and security.

q.q: Why is optical fibre more secure than wireless?
o: Its light signals are very hard to tap, while radio signals can be picked up in range
It uses passwords on every glass strand, while wireless uses no passwords at all
It is always encrypted by law, while wireless data is never allowed to be encrypted
It is slower than wireless, so attackers do not have time to read the data
q.why: Fibre is physically hard to intercept without being detected; wireless signals spread through the air.

q.q: A 500 MB file is sent over a 100 Mbps link. Ignoring overheads, how long does it take?
o: 5 seconds
40 seconds
50 seconds
4 seconds
q.why: 500 × 8 = 4,000 megabits; 4,000 ÷ 100 = 40 seconds. 5 seconds forgets to convert bytes to bits.

q.q: A 4,000 MB file is sent over fibre at 1,000 Mbps. Ignoring overheads, how long does it take?
o: 32 seconds
4 seconds
40 seconds
320 seconds

q.q: A 4,000 MB file is sent over Wi-Fi at 80 Mbps. Ignoring overheads, how long does it take?
o: 50 seconds
400 seconds
320 seconds
3,200 seconds
q.why: 4,000 × 8 = 32,000 megabits; 32,000 ÷ 80 = 400 seconds, nearly 7 minutes.

q.q: A 200 MB file is sent over a 20 Mbps connection. Ignoring overheads, how long does it take?
o: 80 seconds
10 seconds
8 seconds
800 seconds

q.q: Which formula gives the transfer time for a file?
o: File size in megabits ÷ connection speed in megabits per second
Connection speed in megabits per second ÷ file size in megabits
File size in megabytes ÷ connection speed in megabits per second
File size in megabits × connection speed in megabits per second
q.why: The units must match, so convert megabytes to megabits (× 8) first.

q.q: Which is a similarity between wireless and optical fibre communication?
o: Both send data as pulses of light through glass strands in a cable
Both are hard to tap into because signals do not leave the cable
Both carry digital data between devices and can connect to the internet
Both let users move around freely while they stay connected
q.why: Both carry network data; they differ in how the data travels.

q.q: How do many NI homes combine the two technologies for broadband?
o: Wi-Fi to the door, then fibre to each room inside
Bluetooth to the door, then 5G inside the house
Fibre to each device, with no wireless inside
Full fibre to the door, then Wi-Fi inside the house
q.why: Many networks combine fibre to the building with Wi-Fi inside.

q.q: Which is a weakness of optical fibre compared with wireless?
o: Signals are weakened by walls, distance and other devices
Signals can be picked up by anyone within range of them
Fibres can crack if bent sharply, and repairs need specialists
Speed falls as more users connect in the same area
q.why: The other three are weaknesses of wireless.

q.q: Calculated transfer times are ideal figures. Why are real transfers slower?
o: The file size doubles when it is being sent
Fibre must convert each bit into a radio wave
Overheads and other traffic share the connection
The calculation should use bytes, not bits
q.why: Overheads and other users sharing the connection reduce the real speed.

q.q: A school wants to link its main building to a new sports hall 200 m away with a fast, secure connection. What is the best choice?
o: Optical fibre
Bluetooth
4G
Wi-Fi from the main building
q.why: A fixed link needing speed and security suits fibre; Bluetooth's range is only about 10 m.

q.q: Which technology suits a wireless mouse?
o: Bluetooth
4G
Optical fibre
5G
q.why: The mouse is close to the computer and needs low power, so a direct paired link suits it.
